title: Acute respiratory failure: NIV and high-flow nasal oxygen (adult)
subject: critical-care
summary: Use bilevel NIV for COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis persisting after medical therapy and CPAP or NIV for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. In hypoxaemic respiratory failure, prefer high-flow nasal oxygen over conventional oxygen. Reassess early and do not let non-invasive support delay intubation.

sections.title: Assess the type of failure
items: Hypoxaemic (type 1): PaO2 below 60 mmHg (8 kPa) with normal or low PaCO2. Hypercapnic (type 2): PaCO2 above 45 mmHg (6 kPa) with acidosis (pH below 7.35) in acute or acute-on-chronic failure.
Oxygen target: SpO2 88 to 92% if at risk of hypercapnia (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular or chest wall disease); 94 to 98% for most others.
Signs of fatigue: respiratory rate above 30/min, accessory muscle use, abdominal paradox, rising PaCO2, falling GCS.
Treat the cause alongside support: bronchodilators and steroids in COPD, diuretics and nitrates in pulmonary oedema, antibiotics in pneumonia.

sections.title: NIV: when to use (ERS/ATS 2017, BTS 2016)
items: COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.35 or below, PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) persisting despite optimal medical therapy and controlled oxygen: bilevel NIV (strong). BTS: start when pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 6.5 kPa persist or develop.
Severe acidosis alone (for example pH below 7.25) does not preclude an NIV trial, but only where staff who can intubate are immediately available.
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: CPAP or bilevel NIV (strong), including prehospital.

Conditional: immunocompromised patients, post-operative respiratory failure, chest trauma, palliation of dyspnoea in terminal illness, weaning of hypercapnic patients, and prevention of post-extubation failure in high-risk patients.

Not recommended: hypercapnic COPD without acidosis, and treatment of established post-extubation respiratory failure (it delays reintubation). De novo hypoxaemic failure: no ERS/ATS recommendation for NIV.
Obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease and chest wall deformity respond to NIV but often need different settings; seek expert input.

sections.title: NIV set-up and titration
items: Full face mask first. Start IPAP about 15 cmH2O with EPAP of at least 3 cmH2O (the minimum to flush CO2), then raise IPAP to 20 to 30 cmH2O within 10 to 30 minutes as tolerated (BTS).
Raise EPAP for persistent hypoxaemia or upper airway obstruction; obesity hypoventilation often needs IPAP above 30 and EPAP above 8 cmH2O.
Entrain oxygen to the target SpO2; maximise NIV time in the first 24 hours, then taper over 2 to 3 days once pH and PaCO2 normalise.
CPAP for pulmonary oedema: typically 5 to 10 cmH2O.
Before starting, document the plan if NIV fails: is NIV the ceiling of care or a bridge to intubation?

sections.title: High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO)
items: Hypoxaemic failure not due to cardiogenic oedema or COPD exacerbation: HFNO rather than conventional oxygen to reduce intubation (ESICM 2023 strong; ERS 2022 conditional). ERS 2022 also suggests HFNO over NIV here; ESICM makes no recommendation between HFNO and CPAP/NIV.
Settings: flow 30 to 60 L/min (start high), FiO2 titrated to the SpO2 target, humidified at 34 to 37 degrees C.

Use HFNO during breaks from NIV. After extubation: HFNO over conventional oxygen if low risk; NIV rather than HFNO if high risk, unless NIV is contraindicated. After surgery: HFNO or conventional oxygen if low risk; HFNO or NIV if high risk.
Hypercapnic COPD exacerbation: trial NIV first; HFNO is not a substitute (ERS 2022).
COVID-19: CPAP/NIV can be considered instead of HFNO; awake prone positioning is suggested for non-intubated COVID-19 hypoxaemic failure (ESICM).

sections.title: Monitoring and failure criteria
items: Manage in HDU, ICU or a staffed NIV area: continuous SpO2, respiratory rate, heart rate, BP, GCS, synchrony and leak; clinical review within the first hour.

Repeat blood gas within 1 to 2 hours and after each change. Improvement in pH and respiratory rate within 4 hours predicts success; persisting pH below 7.25 with respiratory rate above 35/min predicts failure (BTS).
HFNO: ROX index (SpO2/FiO2 divided by respiratory rate) of 4.88 or more at 2, 6 or 12 hours predicts success; low or falling values should prompt review for intubation.
Hypoxaemic failure on NIV: large expired tidal volumes (above about 9.5 mL/kg predicted body weight) and persisting tachypnoea predict failure.
Before calling NIV a failure, fix technical problems: mask leak, inadequate IPAP, asynchrony, upper airway obstruction.

sections.title: Escalate to intubation
items: Intubate for respiratory or cardiac arrest, falling GCS, inability to protect the airway or clear secretions, haemodynamic instability, or worsening acidosis, hypoxaemia or exhaustion despite optimised support.
Do not let NIV or HFNO delay needed intubation: delayed intubation in hypoxaemic failure is associated with higher mortality.

Contraindications to NIV: arrest, inability to protect the airway, copious secretions or vomiting, upper GI bleeding, facial trauma or burns, undrained pneumothorax, severe agitation; recent upper airway or oesophageal surgery is relative.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen in COPD, worsening hypercapnia.
NIV on a general ward without trained staff, monitoring or an escalation plan.
IPAP left too low, a common cause of NIV failure.
Using NIV to rescue established post-extubation failure instead of reintubating.

drugs.name: Controlled oxygen
drugs.dose: Venturi mask 24 to 28% (or nasal cannula 1 to 2 L/min) titrated to SpO2 88 to 92% in patients at risk of hypercapnia
drugs.notes: Entrain into the NIV circuit to the same target.

drugs.name: Salbutamol (nebulised)
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 5 mg every 20 minutes to 4 hourly as needed
drugs.notes: Air-driven in hypercapnic COPD, or in-line with NIV.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 40 mg orally once daily for 5 days
drugs.notes: COPD exacerbation (IV hydrocortisone if unable to take orally).
